style_when: the story is regulatory or contractual — a filing, a mandate, a rate notice, a certificate, a purchase order that changed the economics
prompt: Overhead flat-lay photograph, top-down 90-degree view of two multiple-choice answer sheets on a graphite desk in a control room, split-screen diptych with a clean vertical seam of empty desk between them. Left: a pristine printed exam sheet, bubbles neatly filled in graphite pencil, a green check stamp at its corner. Right: its re-worded mirror twin, same answer grid but altered question blocks, several bubbles erased and struck through in red ballpoint, a red pen resting across the sheet, rotated slightly out of alignment. Blank, illegibly cropped print, muted paper tones, even diffused daylight from the left, bone white, graphite and oxidised red palette, brushed-steel console edge blurred at the frame, 50mm, fine film grain.
negative_prompt: garbled text, random lettering, legible numbers, watermarks, logos
rationale: The story turns on a named paper artefact — the multiple-choice benchmark sheet — and on the collision between two runs of it, which a top-down flat-lay diptych states at a glance. The green stamp against the red-marked mirror carries the hidden 7.0-point drop without a single legible number, which flux would only garble.
cue: Gate on a fresh mirror run
subject: two multiple-choice answer sheets — a green-stamped original benchmark sheet beside its red-marked re-worded mirror — the published number against the fresh mirror run
core_thesis: A model's published benchmark score is partly memorized test data, so the release decision must gate on a fresh mirror run of re-worded questions — not on the benchmark number and not on a contamination detector.
core_conflict: The green benchmark number (looks like reasoning, but is recall of leaked originals) versus the fresh mirror run on re-worded questions (matched difficulty, honest score) — gating on memorized performance versus gating on the delta between two runs.
composition: split-screen diptych flat-lay with left-right contrast: the original answer sheet on the left, its re-worded mirror on the right, divided by a clean vertical seam of empty desk, the red pen anchoring the right half
